h1: Olive Oil Marinade: What the Oil Is Actually Doing
excerpt: In a marinade the oil is a carrier, not a tenderiser. Here is the ratio against acid, the time each ingredient wants, and which bottle to use.
keyTakeaway: In an olive oil marinade the oil dissolves the fat-soluble aromatics and holds them against the surface of the food. It does not tenderise: salt, the cut and the cooking do that. Three parts oil to one part acid suits meat, more oil for fish, and the clock matters more than the recipe.
heroAlt: A hand holding a bottle of olive oil at the edge of a sunlit olive grove, with a stone ledge and an olive branch in the frame and a path receding between the trees behind.
inlineAlt: A shallow glass dish of raw chicken pieces coated in olive oil marinade, with whole garlic cloves, lemon slices and sprigs of rosemary tucked between them, on a wooden table.
intro: Every marinade recipe opens with olive oil and none says why. The oil does one job, and not the one most people credit it with.
What follows is the mechanism, the ratio against acid, and a timing table by ingredient.

sections.heading: What the oil is doing in there

blocks.text: An olive oil marinade works as a carrier. Most of the flavour in garlic, rosemary, oregano and chilli is fat-soluble, so it dissolves into oil rather than into lemon juice. The oil coats the food and holds that flavour there, through the fridge and onto the heat.

items: **It dissolves the aromatics.** Crushed garlic and bruised rosemary give up more to oil than to juice.
**It stays put.** A thin film holds the seasoning on the meat instead of pooling in the dish.
**It arrives in the pan.** The film clinging to the food browns first.

blocks.text: Olive oil does not tenderise meat. It sits on the outside and travels perhaps a millimetre in, so a marinated steak is seasoned at the surface and unchanged in the middle. Tenderness is settled by five other things, and the oil is none of them.

items: **The cut.** Shin will not become sirloin in a bowl.
**Slicing across the grain.** Shorter fibres, before any cooking.
**Salt.** Reorganises the surface protein and holds water in it.
**Papain.** The enzyme in raw papaya, which overshoots fast.
**Slow cooking.** Low heat breaks down the connective tissue.

blocks.text: A workable olive oil marinade runs about three parts oil to one part acid, with salt and aromatics on top. More acid than that firms and whitens the surface of fish and chicken before any heat reaches it. Less acid and the mixture reads as oily.

items: **3:1 oil to acid** for chicken, lamb and beef.
**4:1 or 5:1** for fish and prawns, which acid reaches within minutes.
**2:1** for firm vegetables and halloumi, with no protein to seize.
**About 2 tbsp of oil per kilo** of food, which puts the acid at roughly 2 tsp.

sections.heading: How long to marinate, by ingredient

blocks.text: Marinating time depends on how far the acid can reach, not on how much flavour is wanted. Fish takes fifteen to thirty minutes. Chicken pieces take two to six hours. A whole beef steak can sit overnight because its surface is dense.

sections.heading: Which bottle goes in the marinade

blocks.text: A whole marinade is not the place for the most expensive bottle in the kitchen. Most of that oil ends up in the dish, on the tray or burning off over the grill, and heat flattens what it carried.

The arithmetic is quick. Two tablespoons per kilo is around 30 ml, and most of it goes with the drips and the smoke rather than onto the plate, so at **RM236** a litre it buys nothing you taste. For the figures, read [olive oil price in Malaysia](/blog/olive-oil-price-in-malaysia-what-you-are-paying-for).

sections.heading: Mix it in the right order

blocks.text: Build the marinade in the dish the food will sit in, and add the olive oil last. Salt dissolves in lemon juice or vinegar and stops dissolving once oil has coated the crystals: acid first, aromatics next, oil whisked in at the end.

items: Stir the salt into the lemon juice or vinegar until it disappears.
Crush the garlic, bruise the herbs, stir them through the acid.
Pour the olive oil in slowly, whisking, until the mixture thickens.
Turn the food through it, cover, and refrigerate for the time it needs.

blocks.text: Olive oil in a marinade dissolves the aromatics and holds them on the surface. Three parts oil to one part acid for meat, more oil still for fish, and the clock matters more than the recipe. See [cooking with olive oil in a Malaysian kitchen](/blog/how-to-cook-with-olive-oil-in-a-malaysian-kitchen).

faqs.a: No. Olive oil coats the surface and travels barely a millimetre in. Tenderness comes from the cut, the direction of the slice, salt, an enzyme such as the one in raw papaya, or slow cooking. A marinade seasons the outer surface only.

faqs.q: How much olive oil against lemon juice in a marinade?
faqs.a: About three parts olive oil to one part lemon juice for chicken, lamb and beef. Move to four or five parts oil for fish and prawns, which acid reaches within minutes. Two tablespoons of oil per kilo of food is enough to coat it.

faqs.q: How long can chicken sit in an olive oil marinade?
faqs.a: Two to six hours for bone-in pieces, thirty minutes to two hours for cubed breast. Beyond that the acid works too far into the surface and the outer layer turns chalky once roasted. Keep the dish covered in the refrigerator, never on the counter.

faqs.q: Can a used marinade be reused?
faqs.a: Not as a sauce and not for a second batch, because raw juices have gone into it. Set part of the mixture aside before the food goes in if a sauce is wanted, or boil the used marinade hard for several minutes first.

faqs.q: Should the good bottle go in the marinade or on the plate?
faqs.a: On the plate. A plain extra virgin oil carries garlic and herbs through the marinade and burns off over the grill, where its aroma is spent. A drizzle after cooking is where the character of a better oil survives, because nothing has heated it.

faqs.q: Do vegetables need marinating before roasting?
faqs.a: Fifteen to forty-five minutes is enough. Vegetables hold no protein for acid to act on, so extra time adds little once the oil has coated every cut face. Toss aubergine, courgette, capsicum and onion with oil, salt and dried oregano before roasting.
